question: Tell me about a time you zoomed out to check whether your day-to-day work still aligned with the mission. What did you find?

raiseTranscript.text: I was fixing small bugs in the checkout flow for a few weeks. During a team retro I stepped back and checked against our mission of making shopping frictionless for first-time users. Most bugs were edge cases for power users, not the core group.
I flagged it to my manager, shifted two of my tickets to onboarding flows, and the conversion rate for new users ticked up 3% in the next sprint.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you zoomed out to check whether your day-to-day work still aligned with the mission. What did you find?
Role: junior dev on checkout bugs
Situation: noticed fixes targeted power users, not new-user mission
Action: raised to manager, reprioritized tickets to onboarding
Outcome: 3% new-user conversion lift
Quote: "I stepped back and checked against our mission of making shopping frictionless for first-time users."
Follow-up: What did you do next? -> Shifted own work, told manager
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Think big, start small for a junior. The candidate described an individual-scope check during a retro that revealed mismatch between bug fixes and the new-user mission. They adjusted their own tickets after a short conversation with their manager. Quote shows they explicitly referenced the mission to reprioritize. This demonstrates ownership and coachability without overclaiming. Biggest strength is the quick pivot from observation to changing their daily work.

lowerTranscript.text: I was just doing the tickets assigned to me in the checkout area.
Did you ever check if those aligned with the bigger mission?
Not really, I figured the PM had already done that.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you zoomed out to check whether your day-to-day work still aligned with the mission. What did you find?

Action: none

No evidence of personal zoom-out or adjustment. Quote shows passive hand-off of thinking. Biggest gap is lack of ownership over even their own work's connection to the mission.

raiseTranscript.text: My team was shipping dashboard widgets while the org mission shifted toward enterprise data governance. I pulled usage data across three partner teams and saw our work was mostly used by internal analysts, not the enterprise customers.
How did you influence the direction?
I wrote a one-pager, ran it by two other team leads, and we moved two quarters of roadmap to governance features. Cross-team adoption of the new primitives rose 40%.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you zoomed out to check whether your day-to-day work still aligned with the mission. What did you find?
Role: senior on dashboard team
Situation: org mission moved to enterprise governance
Action: analyzed cross-team data, wrote one-pager, influenced two other leads
Outcome: roadmap shift, 40% adoption of new primitives
Quote: "I pulled usage data across three partner teams."
Follow-up: How did you influence the direction? -> One-pager and cross-team alignment
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Think big, start small for a senior. Candidate used cross-team data to surface misalignment between widget work and the new enterprise mission. They influenced without authority by sharing a one-pager with peer leads and shifting roadmap. Quote references concrete usage analysis. Result shows measurable adoption lift. Biggest strength is combining personal zoom-out with influence that affected multiple teams.

lowerTranscript.text: I noticed our widgets didn't match the new governance focus but kept shipping because the sprint was already planned.
Did you raise it with anyone?
I mentioned it in a team meeting but the PM said we had committed work so we stayed the course.

Quote shows deference to existing commitments without pushing for trade-offs. No cross-team data or influence attempted. Biggest gap is absence of leverage or follow-through at the senior scope.

raiseTranscript.text: After the company mission pivoted to AI safety, I reviewed our three-year product bets and saw two of them were still optimized for engagement metrics that could conflict with safety goals.

I led a six-week review with the other VPs, killed one bet, and redirected $8M to safety tooling. We published new success metrics that balanced growth and safety; six months later our safety incident rate dropped 25% while revenue stayed flat.

exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Think big, start small for an exec. Candidate performed an org-level review after a mission pivot and identified conflicting bets. Outcome includes both safety gains and revenue protection. Biggest strength is demonstrating judgment on ambiguity and multi-year leverage.
